learning_objectives.description: Describe the relationship between the derivative, slope of the tangent line, instantaneous rate of change, and average rate of change; explain the meaning of the derivative of a function at a given point in context, including determining the units of the derivative; identify and give examples of where a function might not be differentiable graphically; and determine the sign of and compare derivatives based on the graph.

definitions.definition_plain: The derivative of a function f at a number a, denoted f'(a), represents: (i) the slope of the tangent line to the graph of f at the point where x = a; and (ii) the instantaneous rate of change of f in the instant when the input x = a. It is defined by the limit f'(a) = lim as x -> a of (f(x)-f(a))/(x-a) = lim as h -> 0 of (f(a+h)-f(a))/h.
definitions.definition_latex: The \textbf{derivative} of a function $f$ at a number $a$ is denoted by $f'(a)$ and represents: (i) the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $f$ at the point where $x=a$; and (ii) the instantaneous rate of change of $f$ in the instant when the input $x=a$. $$f'(a)=\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$$

definitions.definition_plain: Because the derivative is defined by a limit, sometimes derivatives do not exist. When the limit defining the derivative f'(a) does exist, we say that f is differentiable at a.
definitions.definition_latex: Because the derivative is defined by a limit, sometimes derivatives do not exist. When the limit defining the derivative $f'(a)$ does exist, we say that $f$ is \textbf{differentiable} at $a$.

other_material.content_plain: A function may fail to be differentiable at a point in several ways, including: corners (the slopes of the secant lines from the left and right approach different values); vertical tangents (the secant-line slopes grow without bound, toward +infinity or -infinity); and discontinuities (the secant-line slopes from the two sides differ). In each of these cases the two-sided limit defining f'(a) does not exist, so f'(a) does not exist.
other_material.content_latex: A function may fail to be differentiable at a point in several ways, including: \textbf{corners} (the slopes of the secant lines from the left and right approach different values); \textbf{vertical tangents} (the secant-line slopes grow without bound, toward $+\infty$ or $-\infty$); and \textbf{discontinuities} (the secant-line slopes from the two sides differ). In each case the two-sided limit defining $f'(a)$ does not exist, so $f'(a)$ DNE.

problems.name: Warm-up: Skater's instantaneous velocity

Let f(t) represent the distance travelled (in meters) by a skater around a track at a time t in minutes. In this exercise, we want to learn about the skater's instantaneous velocity at time t = 3 minutes. Since we don't know how to compute this, we'll estimate with average velocity.

The data in this table is plotted on the graph.

t    | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
f(t) | 588.17 | 893.72 | 1052.44 | 1134.9 | 1177.74 | 1200

problems.name: Cost curve: average and instantaneous rate of change
problems.context_plain: A cost curve is a graph depicting the relationship between the total cost C of producing a quantity Q of a particular commodity.
problems.context_latex: A \textbf{cost curve} is a graph depicting the relationship between the total cost $C$ of producing a quantity $Q$ of a particular commodity.

plain_text.question: What does (C(400)-C(200))/(400-200) represent in this context?
plain_text.answer: It represents the average rate of change of the total cost C of production as the quantity Q increases from 200 to 400. That is, the average increase in total cost per 1 unit increase in production between 200 and 400 units of production. Geometrically, it is the slope of the secant line through the points at Q = 200 and Q = 400 on the cost curve.

latex.question: What does $\frac{C(400)-C(200)}{400-200}$ represent in this context?
latex.answer: It represents the average rate of change of the total cost ($C$) of production as quantity ($Q$) increases from $200$ to $400$; i.e. the average increase in total cost per $1$ unit increase in production between $200$ and $400$ units of production. Geometrically, it is the slope of the secant line through $Q=200$ and $Q=400$ on the cost curve.

plain_text.question: What are the units of measurement of the quantity (C(400)-C(200))/(400-200)?
plain_text.answer: dollars per unit of Q ($ / units of Q)

latex.question: What are the units of measurement of the quantity $\frac{C(400)-C(200)}{400-200}$?

plain_text.question: What does lim as Q -> 200 of (C(Q)-C(200))/(Q-200) represent in this context?
plain_text.answer: It represents the instantaneous rate of change of the total cost of production (C) when 200 units of Q are produced. This is the expected increase in total cost per 1 unit increase in production if cost continues to change exactly as it did when 200 units were produced. In economics, this quantity is the marginal cost. Geometrically, it is the slope of the tangent line to the cost curve at Q = 200.

latex.question: What does $\displaystyle\lim_{Q\to200}\frac{C(Q)-C(200)}{Q-200}$ represent in this context?
latex.answer: It represents the instantaneous rate of change of the total cost of production ($C$) when $200$ units of $Q$ are produced; the expected increase in total cost per $1$ unit increase in production if cost continues to change exactly as it did when $200$ units were produced. In economics, this quantity is \emph{marginal cost}. Geometrically, it is the slope of the tangent line to the cost curve at $Q=200$.

plain_text.question: What are the units of measurement of the quantity lim as Q -> 200 of (C(Q)-C(200))/(Q-200)?
plain_text.answer: dollars per unit of Q ($ / units of Q)

problems.context_plain: A particle travels along the x-axis such that its position (in centimeters) along the axis at time t (in seconds) is given by the function p(t).
problems.context_latex: A particle travels along the $x$-axis such that its position (in centimeters) along the axis at time $t$ (in seconds) is given by the function $p(t)$.

plain_text.question: What are the units of measurement of p'(t)?

latex.question: What are the units of measurement of $p'(t)$?

plain_text.question: Write a sentence describing what p'(t) represents in this context. (Note: "in this context" means your answer must clearly relate to the scenario described in the problem - a curve relating position p and time t. Answers like "the derivative of p" are not in this context.)
plain_text.answer: The instantaneous velocity of the particle at time t seconds. The particle is traveling p'(t) cm/sec at time t seconds.
